name: ePTFE (Gore-Tex) facial implant
lead: Expanded polytetrafluoroethylene (ePTFE), best known under the brand name Gore-Tex, is a flexible, porous synthetic material used in facial implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose, as well as in many non-cosmetic medical devices. Expanded PTFE was produced in 1969 by Robert Gore, who rapidly stretched heated PTFE to create a microporous structure; because it is nearly inert in the body and allows tissue to grow into it, it is used in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches and other implants [1].

In chin augmentation, ePTFE is described as flexible, strong and porous, fixed to bone with titanium screws, with tissue ingrowth providing most of the hold [2]. Published cosmetic studies in the reviewed material are limited: a 1997 evaluation of Gore-Tex lip augmentation [3], a literature review of ePTFE in rhinoplasty that notes both advocates and opponents of alloplast use [4], and a comparison study in Asian nasal dorsal augmentation [5].
infobox: Chin, lips, nasolabial folds, nasal dorsum [2][3][4]

paras: Expanded PTFE is chemically inert, thermally stable and has tunable porosity; it is about 70% air in the Gore-Tex membrane form [1]. In the body it is used in vascular grafts, sutures, heart patches, synthetic ligaments and glaucoma surgery membranes [1].
Among chin implants, ePTFE is listed with silicone and porous polyethylene as the commonly used synthetic options [2][6].

The material was developed in 1969 by Bob Gore, son of W. L. Gore, who accelerated the stretching of heated PTFE rods so that it expanded roughly 800% into a microporous structure. Gore patents were upheld in 1983 and the company's ePTFE fabric patents expired in 1997 [1].

A review in Facial Plastic Surgery describes ePTFE as having attracted attention in rhinoplasty over about 30 years, from both advocates and opponents, with surgeon hesitation about alloplasts based on historical data from earlier nasal implants [4].
Chin: described as flexible, strong and porous, attached with titanium screws [2].
Lips: a 1997 study in Aesthetic Plastic Surgery evaluated lip augmentation with a Gore-Tex facial implant [3].

Nose: the rhinoplasty review notes that objective large-series long-term data are needed to settle the debate over its use [4], and a 2010 study asked whether ePTFE is an alternative material for nasal dorsal augmentation in Asians [5].

Studies identified are small clinical series and reviews. A 1997 study evaluated lip augmentation with Gore-Tex [3]; a literature review covers ePTFE in rhinoplasty, including techniques and outcomes [4]; and a 2010 paper addresses nasal dorsal augmentation in Asian patients [5].

Most other published ePTFE studies concern non-cosmetic uses, such as laryngeal vocal fold medialization [7][8], glaucoma surgery with a randomised trial of mitomycin-C [9].  A registered trial of Gore-Tex implants for atrophic rhinitis was suspended (n=5) [10]. These are noted for context and do not examine appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: Gore patents upheld in Gore v. Garlock.[1]
Gore ePTFE fabric patents expire; a study on Gore-Tex lip augmentation is published.[1][3]

card.summary: Gore-Tex-type porous synthetic implant used for chin, lip, nasolabial and nasal augmentation; cosmetic studies are small and mostly older.
card.note: Porous material that tissue grows into; cosmetic evidence limited to small series and reviews.

quick.overview:
Expanded PTFE, sold as Gore-Tex, is a flexible porous synthetic used in implants for the chin, lips, nasolabial folds and nose. It was developed in 1969 and is widely used elsewhere in medicine, for example in grafts and sutures.

Cosmetic evidence in the reviewed material is limited to a lip-augmentation study, a rhinoplasty literature review and an Asian nasal dorsum study.
quick.mechanism: The microporous material is shaped and placed in a pocket, in the chin attached to bone with titanium screws, and tissue grows into its pores to help hold it [2].
quick.risks: General implant risks include swelling, infection, displacement and nerve injury. Surgeons quoted in the rhinoplasty review express hesitation about alloplast use because of historical experience with earlier nasal implants [4].
